# ODD Task — Phase 9: Consolidation and polish

> **Roadmap authority:** [Standalone Platform Master Roadmap](../../openspec/decisions/standalone-platform-roadmap.md), canonical **Phase 9 — Consolidation and polish** (inserted by the user on 2026-10-01): pay down the debt Phases 5–8 deferred — the SDD/ODD skill rewrite for labdrian's sub-agent team and the deferred cleanup backlog — before building Observability (Phase 10) and Release (Phase 11).

## Problem and why

Phases 5–8 shipped with a recorded backlog of deferred items, an approval baseline that exempts 27 skills failing the lint budget, and skills that were written for a single agent rather than a team of role agents. The user decided the cleanup must not be left out, and set a governing principle: the whole system must align with hexagonal architecture and clean code to the maximum, whatever it costs.

## Inventory

Ultracode workflow `wf_afe65bf2-736` (9 read-only agents) collected 124 items from Engram, the Phase 5–8 ledgers, the skills, and repository state, and verified each against `main` `f19a33c` (Engram #3855). Items proven fixed were removed with their proof (install-hooks summary `28d2082`; workflow store flake `a6d10dc`; #309 and #312 code items; Phase 5 residuals C3/C4; SL2 `--pre`).

## Decisions (user, 2026-10-01)

- **Principle:** hexagonal architecture and clean code to the maximum, whatever it costs; every design fork offers and prefers the maximum-decoupling option (Engram #3856).
- **Q1 hook upgrade:** `install-hooks` replaces owned entries in place when their command changes; a test pins that old unquoted entries are recognized as owned.
- **Q2 upstream core skills:** create new overlay-owned role skills for the sub-agent team; leave the 15 upstream core skills untouched; document them in the vault as sources.
- **Q3 untracked tool directories:** `.gitignore` `.agents/`, `.claude/skills/`, `.pi/`, `skills-lock.json`; resolve the tracked `skills/archify` symlink to untracked content.
- **Q4 #293 frozen promoted pages:** doctor-only report with the explicit-promote / pin remedy.
- **Q5 #312 registry/engine coupling:** the skills domain reads its own registry model through a port; the YAML file is an adapter; tolerant reader with must-understand fields; versioned adapters for format changes.
- **Q6 profile retirement:** snapshot the resolved profile into the workflow log at creation; workflows are self-contained; the catalog only serves new workflows.
- **Q7 runtime adapters:** archive `runtime-roster` as superseded; implement R-141 as an `Adapter` port with a self-registering adapter registry; an unregistered target is an error.
- **Q8 project identity:** a `ProjectIdentity` port with ordered adapters (explicit `--project-id`, origin remote read from `.git/config` without running git, directory name). (The "verb to declare project-scoped skills (R-046/R-047)" first written here was a misreading: R-046/R-047 of `skill-project-scope` are identity rules, superseded by this chain on 2026-10-06, and project-scoped skills are declared with `skills project-register`, Phase 8.)
- **Q9 open SDD changes:** archive `overlay-versioned-releases`; finish `longterm-mem-knowledge-ingestion` as an adapter behind an ingestion port, before the skills documentation.
- **Q10 orphan branches:** delete `pr137`, `feat/archive-reconcile-guard`, `fix/ci-full-history-for-engine-tests` (superseded on main); keep `wip/audit-remediation-snapshot` (review it) and `sdd/shared-project-vault` (input for the vault work).
- **Q11 additions:** `.gitattributes` `skills/** -text`; a deadline on the Pi subprocess through an injected `CommandRunner` port; a real `memory:procedural-skills` signal through a project-context port; a guarded sandbox test of the Pi global tier. OpenCode `skills` stays `partial`.
- **Q12 goal-v2 open question:** close as superseded.
- **Vault (user):** the skills analysis lives in the project vault `~/labdrian-brain` (registered in `~/.labdrian-overlay/vaults.json`): one page per skill and per role, comparisons, open questions; research and thinking happen there; the new skills are designed from that knowledge. The user's uncommitted `.obsidian/` changes are never touched.

## Scope and constraints

- Hexagonal principle governs every task. TDD strict (`go test` from `engine/` and `longterm-mem/`). RDD on. One slice at a time. Candidates under about 150 KB.
- Tests never touch real state. Destructive, GitHub, deploy, vault-write, and `~/.codex` steps each need explicit approval at the time.
- Ultracode: the user opted into multi-agent workflows for this phase.

An unreadable store is a `*skills.RegistryReadError` and returns the zero registry. **Moved.** `parse.go` and `serialize.go` to `registryyaml/decode.go` and `encode.go` (history kept), their tests and testdata with them (`skills:TestSerializeRoundTripRealRegistry` is `registryyaml:TestEncodeRoundTripRealRegistry`, `skills:TestSerializeGoldenTwoEntry` is `registryyaml:TestEncodeGoldenTwoEntry`; the citation in `openspec/decisions/standalone-platform-roadmap.md` is fixed); the vocabulary of a registry (`ScopeGlobal`, `SourceCore`, ...) and `RegistryTargets()` live in the domain. **Call sites.** Every verb of `skills` (`list`, `status`, `skills`, `lifecycle`, `sync`, `install`, `project_cli`, `match`) takes the repository after `readFile`; `RenderListCore` and `RenderStatusCore` take it instead of `readFile`; `pipkg` and the Pi runtime adapter read through the port they are given (a file- or directory-backed registry); `cmd/registry_repository.go` constructs the adapter and is the one place that does. The tests of package `skills` cannot import the adapter (an import cycle in a test), so `export_test.go` and an external `skills_test` file register it when the test binary starts. **Closed by H15:** the `parse` and `serialize` call sites, `pipkg-registry-direct-parse`. The two checks the adapter keeps because they name a line (a scope outside its two words, a source that contradicts its type) are checks of the file, worded with the line they are on, and the domain holds every registry to the same rules again.
  - **H16** (`1045cce`; Q5, no new decision). **Closes #312.** The file's `version` selects the decoder (`decoders`, one per version, with the field table of each in `schemas`); the reader is tolerant of what it does not know; a fixed set of fields is never read without being understood. **The version rule.** The version is found first (the value of the top-level key `version`; the last one if the file says it twice, as before), a version no decoder is for is refused naming it (`skills: version "2" is not supported; only version "1" is valid`, and `the valid versions are "1", "2"` when there are several) before anything else is read, and a file with none is refused for that before any fault of its entries. A change to the format that a reader of the version before would misread is a new version with a new decoder beside the old ones; a change that only adds a field is not. **Unknown fields.** A key the reader does not know, in any mapping, is left out and said: `Registry.Unread` holds one note per field (`line 7: unknown key "mirror" in source`), what is under it is skipped, and a key that repeats inside a mapping is still refused as a duplicate. The verbs that read warn on stderr (`warning: registry fields left unread: <first> (and N more)`, so a script that reads stdout is not changed) and go on; `AddEntry`, `RemoveEntry` (first thing they check) and the adapter's `Encode` refuse a registry that has one, because writing it back would drop it. `pipkg` reads the registry too and does not warn: it builds from `id`, `path` and `install.targets`, all of the set. **The must-understand set of version 1,** computed from the schema table the decoder reads (`registryyaml.MustUnderstand("1")`), found by reading what consumes each field, and written with one line of rationale per field at the top of `registryyaml/doc.go` (a test holds that list to the code): `version` selects the decoder; `skills` the entries (a value there is not an empty list); `id` names the skill in the install directory and the project lock; `path` is the directory the skill is read from and the containment boundary of install and `pipkg`; `source` holds `source.type`; `source.type` decides the manifest tag (managed or custom), so how `sync-manifest` and `validate` treat the skill; `install` holds the scope, the projects and the targets; `install.defaultScope` is where it is installed, and a scope read as none skips the approval check (`approval_gate.go`); `install.allowedProjects` are the projects `install` admits a project skill to, and read as empty admits it to none; `install.targets` are the runtimes it is projected to (the Pi package, `list`). Not in the set, because nothing decides on them: `source.upstream` and its owner, `source.repo`, `source.ref` (provenance, which only the domain's rule on the source type looks at) and `lifecycle` with `updateStrategy` (shown by `list`, required by the domain's rule). **The shape rule.** A field is read in its own shape (a scalar has no block under it; a block or a list has no value on its line). A field of the set in another shape is refused, naming the field and the line (`line 5: source must be a block of fields (type, upstream, repo, ref), not a value`); any other field has the wrong part left out and said (the block under a scalar is skipped; the value on the line of a block is noted and the block under it is read, as it always was without a word). **Every behavior difference from the strict reader,** each pinned: (1) a key the reader does not know is read around and said (was a refusal; 330 of the generated documents), at the root, in an entry, a source, an upstream, an install and a lifecycle; (2) `add` and `remove` refuse such a registry, naming what would be lost; (3) the version is judged before the entries: an invalid entry before a version the file gets wrong now names the version, a file with no version and a mis-indented entry names the missing version, and a file whose first line is indented, or a byte-order mark before `version`, says the version is missing (was `unexpected indentation at document root` and `unknown top-level key "\ufeffversion"`); (4) `version:` with no value says `version "" is not supported` (was `unknown top-level key "version"`); (5) a field of the set in a shape it does not read is refused by name: `skills: nope` (was `unknown top-level key "skills"`), and an inline value on the line of `source`, `install`, `install.targets` or `install.allowedProjects`, which the strict reader ignored while it read the block under it, is now refused (139 documents the old reader accepted, none of any other kind), and a block under `version`, `id`, `path`, `source.type` or `install.defaultScope` is refused by name (was `unexpected indentation`); (6) the value on the line of `source.upstream` or `lifecycle` is read as before and now noted (35 documents), and a block under `source.upstream.owner`, `source.repo`, `source.ref` or `lifecycle.updateStrategy` is left out and noted (was `unexpected indentation`), after which the domain still refuses what it requires (an owner for a core skill's upstream, a repository for an external source, an update strategy); (7) consequences of (1) in the words of a refusal: a source with no type but a stray key, a lifecycle with no strategy but a stray key, an upstream with only a stray key, and an unknown key before an invalid scope now name what the domain finds, not the stray key; (8) an unknown key that repeats at the root is told twice, because the strict reader never checked the root for a key that repeats (the same quirk as `version` and `skills` twice, kept: the last wins). **Goldens changed: 19 files (34 case blocks) and 4 new.** Thirteen files hold the state of the harness "a registry with a key the reader does not know" (`mirror: x` in a source), which every verb meets: the same input now exits 0 with the warning for `list`, `status`, `install`, `adopt`, `sync-manifest`, `project-register`, `-retire`, `-status`, `pipkg build` and `check` and the Pi adapter, and refuses to write for `add` and `remove`; So the witness cleanup of `ca5f0db` would hang the test forever, instead of failing it, when the descendant survived, the reader's cleanup `Close` would hang the same way, and the comments that said closing ends a pending read were false. `R3-001` (the dependency only moved) and `R2-001`: the `WaitGroup` is gone. Each goroutine owns its file and its signal: the reader goroutine reads the program's ready line and then the end of the FIFO, closes the reader itself once its reads returned and closes `readerDone`; the witness cleanup owns the goroutine that reads the witness and closes the witness only after that read returned; the run of the program has `runnerDone`. A cleanup waits for a signal with `awaitDone` (bounded by `descendantGoneWait`), reports what outlived the wait and leaves that goroutine blocked, never closing under a read. The cleanups run in the order cancel and wait for the run, close the write end, kill, read the witness, wait for the reader goroutine. Every remaining goroutine is one of these three; none is counted outside the goroutine's owner. Mutations: with the kill cleanup and `ownProcessGroup` removed and both waits at 3 s, the test fails within the bounds (three reports: the descendant held the FIFO, the program or its descendant still running, the reader goroutine still running) and does not hang (run under `timeout 120`); the reader error path (the first read replaced by an error) fails once, with the injected error, and leaves nothing behind. `-race -count=10` passes.

Both are in `pipkgGitOptions`, and a test says so. **Decision 1, the environment git sees (recommendation: scrub the variables that locate a repository).** Evidence in the comparison below: with `GIT_DIR` pointing at another repository in the environment, both binaries compare the package against that repository (`compared against main (c4667eb07131) ... skills/pi-skill/SKILL.md: changed`); a git hook that runs `pipkg check` sets exactly that. I recommend removing `GIT_DIR`, `GIT_WORK_TREE`, `GIT_INDEX_FILE`, `GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY`, `GIT_ALTERNATE_OBJECT_DIRECTORIES`, `GIT_COMMON_DIR`, `GIT_NAMESPACE` and `GIT_PREFIX` and keeping everything else (`PATH`, `HOME`, `GIT_CONFIG_*`, the locale, the Windows variables git needs) rather than an allowlist, which breaks on a platform whose variables nobody listed; it is one function in `cmd` and the adapter does not change. It is a behavior change, so it waits for the owner. **Decision 2, a deadline on git (recommendation: two minutes a call).** Nothing stops a hung `git` today (a lock, a network file system), as nothing stopped `pi`. Every call the builder makes is local and takes milliseconds except `status --untracked-files=all` and `archive`, which take seconds on a large tree; two minutes is far above that and finite. It is `Options.Timeout` in `pipkgGitOptions`, zero today. It is a behavior change (a git that ran longer would be reported as a failure), so it waits for the owner too.
  - **Behavior of the frontmatter: four differences, all on input that was malformed or odd, classified.** The build and the Pi link now read with the lint's fence rules. (1) A SKILL.md or GADU.md that starts with a byte-order mark is accepted; it was refused as "no frontmatter block" / "missing opening --- delimiter". (2) A key that is indented under another key is no longer a top-level one: `metadata:\n  name: x` used to satisfy the build's name check, and `metadata:\n  description: x` the link's description check. (3) A SKILL.md whose block is never closed is refused (`frontmatter is not terminated`) even when a `name:` came first. (4) A fence that is indented is not a fence. Real files are unaffected (the real overlay and `pipkg-real-repo` below are byte-identical). The CHANGELOG says it.

What the suggestion was after, that the loop mutate shared state inline and obscure that only the prober differs, is fixed: `hookWorld.envWithEverythingPresent()` is `env()` plus the prober, named and documented, and the case reads `e := w.envWithEverythingPresent()`.   - **Q6, taken literally.** The workflow's created event records a snapshot of the profile as the catalog gave it, and the workflow is self-contained from then on; the catalog only serves a new workflow (`Create`) and a request (`memory plan --profile`).
  - **The v2 event, as designed (written down here after the tests that pin it, which were written before the code).** `WorkflowEvent.Version` is 1 or 2 (`EventVersionNameOnly`, `EventVersionSnapshot`; `EventVersion` is the one written for a new workflow, 2). A log has the version of its created event from its first line to its last: `State.Version` is set by the created event, `CheckTransition` refuses an event of another version with `ErrMixedVersions`, so `ClassifyLog` classifies such a log as drifted and `AdmitAppend` refuses to extend it, and the lifecycle appends events of the log's version (`eventWith`: the version of the replayed state, the current one for a log that does not exist). So a v1 log is never rewritten or mixed: it stays v1 to its close. The version 2 created event adds two fields, written after `profile` and before `role_chain_id`: `"profile_snapshot"` (an object, `omitempty` as a pointer) and `"profile_digest"` (a string, `omitempty`); a version 1 event omits both, so its bytes are as they were. `profile_snapshot` is `workflowprofile.Snapshot`: `{"name","stages":[{"name","depends_on":[...]}],"roles","checks","memory_policy","review_policy","delivery_policy","memory_default":{"scope","sources":[...]},"relies_on_gentle_review"}`, all of what `Validate`, `RecordStage`, `Verify`, `observationsFor` (the dependencies recorded) and the projection read of a profile (the seven wire fields and the typed data of H32). Lists are never null (an empty list is `[]`; `Snapshot.Validate` refuses a null one, so one profile has one encoding). `profile_digest` is the SHA-256, lowercase hex, of `json.Marshal(snapshot)`: the compact encoding of the struct with its fields in declaration order and `encoding/json`'s escaping, the same encoding rule `EventDigest` uses for the event. Validation of a version 2 created event, with no look at the catalog: `profile` a safe identifier; the snapshot present, of the profile the event names, well formed (`Snapshot.Validate`: the seven fields populated, stages named once and depending only on earlier ones, lists present, a known memory scope and known sources) and within bounds (at most `MaxStages` stages, names within `MaxStageLength`, at most `MaxProfileListLength` (64) roles and checks, every text within `MaxProfileTextLength` (4096 runes)); and the digest equal to the snapshot's. A version 2 verified event's `checked.profile` is a safe name, and `CheckTransition` requires it to be the workflow's profile (version 1 never compared them and still does not). A version 1 created event must hold neither field and still names a catalog profile. `ParseWorkflowEvent` checks unknown keys inside the snapshot, each stage and the memory default, exact case. The pins: `TestAVersion2CreatedEventIsEncodedAsRecorded` (the line written out by hand, its event digest the SHA-256 of those bytes), `TestASnapshotIsEncodedAndDigestedAsRecordedInTheLog` (the encoding by hand, its digest computed outside the program with `printf | sha256sum`), `TestAVersion1EventIsEncodedWithoutTheSnapshotFields`.
  - **Every consumer of a profile identified by name, and where each went.** `rg` over the non-test code finds these name lookups now: `workflow.ProfileOf(state, catalog)` (the snapshot if the log has one, else `catalog.Resolve(state.Profile)`), used by `Lifecycle` (Start, Pause, Resume, Close through `stateEvent`; RecordStage; Verify) and by `projection` (`profileOf`: `nextStage`, `resolvePlan` for the context and the memory gate); `Lifecycle.Create` (the catalog serves the new workflow); `cmd/memory.go` (`memory plan --profile`, a request); `workflow.go` (the version 1 validation of a created and a verified event); `DetectProfileDrift` (the comparison). The reads of the name for display (`projection/gate.go`, the status JSON in `cmd/workflow.go`) are unchanged. The consumer the plan did not name and that mattered: the projection (the prompt hook's next stage and memory plan, and the PreToolUse memory gate). Left on the catalog, a drifted version 2 workflow would have been advanced by the lifecycle from its snapshot while the hooks told the agent the catalog's next stage and enforced the catalog's memory ceiling.
  - **What moved where.** `workflowprofile/snapshot.go` (new): `Snapshot`, `WorkflowProfile.Snapshot()`, `Snapshot.Profile()` (a conversion, so a field added to one type and not the other does not build), `Digest`, `Validate`, `DifferingFields`; `checkShape` extracted from `Validate` (same messages, same order); `MemoryDefault` got json tags (the profile still serializes its seven fields: `MemoryDefault` on the profile stays `json:"-"`). `workflow`: `EventVersionNameOnly/Snapshot`, `MaxProfileTextLength/ListLength`, the two event fields, `validateCreatedProfile`, `validateSnapshotBounds`, `validateCheckedProfile`, `checkNestedSnapshotFields`; `State.Version`, `State.ProfileSnapshot`, `ErrMixedVersions`; `ProfileOf`, `profileOf`, `stateEvent`; `drift.go`: `ProfileDrift`, `ProfileDriftKind` (`changed`, `retired`), `DetectProfileDrift`, `Lifecycle.ProfileDrift`; the `ProfileCatalog` port says an unknown profile wraps `workflowprofile.ErrUnknownProfile`. `projection/context.go`: `profileOf(state)`; `nextStage`, `resolvePlan`, `memoryPlanLines` take the state. The log adapter (`workflow/filelog`) did not change: it only reads and writes the lines the domain classifies and admits.
  - **Pins first.** `59876df`, `90f8880` and `b10ec0e`: ten v1 logs written by the unchanged program (the program built at `582896b`; five profiles, each created-only and running with two stages; one world each under a throwaway root; the script is outside the repository, as `compare_profiles.py` was) and `TestWorkflowV1Golden`: for each profile, the log of the running workflow continued through the other stages (the first again, an undeclared one and the last refused), a verify, a completed close and the status, and the log of the created workflow through a refused stage, a refused pause, a start, a second start refused, a pause, a refused stage, a resume, a stage, a verify and an abandoned close; every exit code, both streams, and the log line by line as version, seq, kind and the SHA-256 of the line with the timestamp and the chain digests masked (the lines are about a kilobyte each). Plus the hook case `prompt-and-gate-follow-a-version-1-log-of-every-profile`. They pass unchanged after every later commit, as do the profile and hook goldens of H32.
  - **Binary comparison.** `engine-old` (`582896b`) and `engine-new` (the tip) in throwaway worlds (HOME, state, PATH and working directory under one temporary root): for each of the five profiles, a fresh workflow through its whole life, a v1 log written by the old binary (running with two stages) continued by both, and a v1 log (created only) taken through pause, resume and an abandoned close by both; 205 pairs of invocations. **Old against new: no difference** in any exit code, stream or log event. The logs of the fresh workflows equal each other once `version` is set to 1, the two snapshot fields removed and the timestamps and chain digests masked; the new log is version 2 with the snapshot on the created event alone; the new binary never wrote a version 2 event into a v1 log. The control (the old binary run as the new) is flagged for the five fresh workflows, so the comparison can fail.
  - **Differences, all classified.** (a) Fresh workflows: the log of a new workflow is version 2 and its created event holds `profile_snapshot` and `profile_digest`: the recorded, deliberate format change (CHANGELOG). Nothing printed differs. (b) A version 1 log: none. (c) Downgrade: the old binary reads a version 2 log as `classification: foreign` (exit 0, an empty state) and refuses to append to it; a workflow created by this version is not to be carried on by an older program (CHANGELOG says so). (d) For a caller that builds a lifecycle over its own catalog, a new workflow's snapshot is what that catalog returns, and the dependencies it records follow it (unchanged since H32). (e) `Create` with a catalog that returns a profile of another name than asked is refused by the created event's validation (before, it recorded the requested name).

Two guards survived and were removed as redundant, with the proof: the 64-hex test of `profile_digest` (the digest is compared with the one computed, which is always 64 lowercase hex) and the `profile.Name != profileName` check in `Create` (the created event's own validation refuses it).
  - **Decision stopped on: how drift is surfaced to the user (a product decision).** The finding exists, is typed and is tested (`workflow.ProfileDrift{Kind changed|retired, Profile, RecordedDigest, CurrentDigest, Fields}`, `workflow.DetectProfileDrift(state, catalog)`, `Lifecycle.ProfileDrift(project, workflow)`), and changes the behavior of no verb. No command prints it yet, because the choice among a warning in `status`, a refusal, or a new verb is the owner's. Recommendation: an additive field on `workflow status` (`"profile_drift": {"kind", "profile", "fields"}`, omitted when there is none, so every version 1 status and every undrifted version 2 status keeps its bytes) and one warning line on stderr of `workflow verify`, which still succeeds with exit 0; no refusal (the workflow is self-contained by decision Q6, and a refusal would make the snapshot worthless), no new verb (a read-only report belongs to `status`). The prompt hook would not mention it (a hook that names the catalog's change to an agent that cannot act on it is noise). The wiring is one small commit in `cmd/workflow.go` plus a golden once this is decided.

The script path, the timeout, the trimming, the exit-code and the empty-output checks moved to `internal/vault/address.go` as `vault.AddressAllocator{Root}` with `NextAddress() (string, error)`; promote owns the port (`AddressAllocator`) and `Writer.Addresses`; `cmd/longterm-mem/rundeps.go` (`runPromote`, used by `promote` and the MCP tool) and `cmd_sync.go` wire the adapter. Other `vault` users in `cmd` (`Rebuild`, `Retrieve`, `Provisioned`, `PrerequisitePresent`) are unchanged: promote never used them. The allocation logic that stays in promote is the part that reads the vault's pages and the manifest (reuse of a page's own address, `recordAddress`), owed to L3. *Clock:* `nowFunc` had 5 readers: `EmitPage` (the created/updated day), `recordAddress` (the day a new manifest is seeded), `Writer.register` (the log entry), `writeSyncState` (the completion instant) and, through them, `Writer.Promote` and `Sync`. `EmitPage` and `Allocate` take the instant as an argument (the Writer reads it from `Writer.Clock`, `Sync` from the same writer); `Clock` is a port promote owns, `cmd/longterm-mem/clock.go` is the adapter (`utcClock`, the wall clock in UTC), and promote converts to UTC itself so the date rule does not depend on the adapter. Decided and done in `c679cf1`: `promote.UnreadablePage` is a page the scan could not read; `scanPromotedPages` skips it and keeps it apart (`pageScan.unreadable`) instead of failing; a pages directory that cannot be listed, or a reader that was not wired, is still the failure of every lookup (golden `12` is unchanged), and `UnreadablePages` (the survey `Sync` and `Plan` name the pages from) returns none for them so that those failures are reported as they were. **What a skipped page means for an observation.** The page's frontmatter cannot be read, so which observation it is the page of is unknown. `findPromotedPage` therefore has three answers: a readable page carries the observation (promoted, as ever, whatever else cannot be read: that page cannot also be its page, or it would have two); no page carries it and nothing was unreadable (not promoted, as ever); no readable page carries it and a page could not be read, which is `unreadablePagesError`, "the state is unknown". An observation in the third state is left alone: no address is taken, nothing is written (not the page, the address map, the sidecar, the catalog or the log), and it is never re-created at a new address beside a page that may be its own. `Writer.Promote` reports it as `ActionSkippedUnreadablePages` (`skipped_unreadable_pages`, a skip with a `Diagnostic` naming the observation and every unreadable page and its cause, and no page), `Sync` and `Plan` as `Withheld` (not a failure and not counted as skipped), `Propagate` as `Withheld`; in `Propagate` a superseded observation whose successor's page is unknown gets its status with `related` empty, as for a successor with no page, because the status is the warning and a later run adds the link. The consequence, said plainly: while one page cannot be read, every observation without a readable page of its own (a never promoted one, and the ineligible ones the propagation pass walks) is left alone, because none of them can be told from the unreadable page's; repairing or removing the page ends it. **Exit code.** The convention that exists is `exitRegistrationConflict` (6): "an artifact already occupies the target location and longterm-mem cannot prove it wrote it, so it refused and changed nothing", which is what `promote --id` answers for a refused edit (`refused <address> (skipped_local_edit)`); the same code is reused. `promote --id` of an observation left alone prints `longterm-mem: refused observation N (skipped_unreadable_pages)` on stdout, the diagnostic on stderr and exits 6. `sync` and `sync --dry-run` do everything else (promote what can be promoted, patch, rebuild the index, record the sync state) and exit 6 when an observation was left alone and nothing failed; a failure still outranks (1, 4 or 5 as before), and a skipped page with no observation left alone (a project with no observation without a page) is only named, exit 0. `sync` has no earlier partial-skip code: its refusal of an edit (`skipped_local_edit`) is counted as promoted and exits 0, a quirk that is pre-existing and not changed here, so 6 for sync is the extension by analogy of the one code the binary uses for "refused, wrote nothing", and the one to change if the owner prefers 1 or a new code. The new output, exactly (golden `04`; `05` is the same with the cause `read <vault>/wiki/memory/c-000901.md: is a directory`): `promote --id 1` exit 6, stdout `longterm-mem: refused observation 1 (skipped_unreadable_pages)`, stderr `longterm-mem: promote: observation 1 was not promoted: no readable page belongs to it, but a page that could not be read may: promoted page c-000901.md could not be read: open <vault>/wiki/memory/c-000901.md: no such file or directory; nothing was written for it`; `sync` exit 6, stdout unchanged (`longterm-mem: sync promoted 0 observation(s), patched 0 page(s)`), stderr `longterm-mem: sync: warning: promoted page c-000901.md could not be read: open <vault>/wiki/memory/c-000901.md: no such file or directory; it was skipped`, `longterm-mem: sync: warning: 2 observation(s) left alone, nothing was written for them: no readable page belongs to them, and a page that could not be read may (observations 1, 2)` and `longterm-mem: sync: warning: 4 observation(s) left alone, nothing was patched for them: ... (observations 1, 2, 3, 4)`. Consumers enumerated: the cmd goldens `04`, `05` (re-recorded; `12` and the other 20 of the 23 recorded before are byte for byte unchanged, and the vault bytes of `04` and `05` are unchanged); `engine/synctrigger` classifies a sync exit code and logs `failure:exit-6` instead of `failure:exit-1` for such a run, a log line and nothing else; the MCP `promote` tool answers `Action: skipped_unreadable_pages` with no address, as it answers `skipped_local_edit` (and no longer an error); `reindexAfterPromote` writes nothing for it. Root cause: the goldens were recorded on 2026-10-10 and masked the date as `<today>`, but the precedence sidecar's `frontmatter_hash` is a hash of page frontmatter that contains the date, so the recorded hash was only true on the day of the recording (promote-golden step 01: want `d0e83d33b606...`, got `2c84a9e48058...`). The mask hid the date in the text and could not reach the hash. Fix: `96b6a07` makes the clock an injected part of `commands` (`productionCommands` composes `utcClock{}`; `promote`, `sync` and the MCP promote tool hand it to `newPromoteWriter`), and `0ee0f2c` runs the golden worlds with a clock fixed at 2026-10-10T12:00:00Z, so the recorded hashes hold on any day; the goldens now show the real date, and the only change to them is mask to literal (254 lines, proved by diff: each removed line with `<today>` and `"last_sync_completed_at": "<now>"` replaced by the literals equals the added line; no hash line changed). The midnight-crossing normaliser of batch 30 is removed, and `<now>` stays only for the provisioned sentinel, which the vault writes from the wall clock, masked by its position. Every other test of the class was checked: the ops goldens, `main_test.go` and the reconcile tests render pages at fixed instants (`testdata.Instant()`, `fixtureInstant`), so no other hash, size or byte count derives from the day.

Current, for a ledger that does not match its digest (golden 50, stderr, after the line that says what was resolved): `WARN stale: this repository's identity ledger could not be read (identityledger: ledger does not match its own digest: <file> carries sha256:A but its entries digest to sha256:B), so an identity the memory already uses may have been missed` and then `WARN stale: this repository's identity ledger could not be written (identityledger: ledger does not match its own digest: <file> carries sha256:A but its entries digest to sha256:B), so an identity the memory already uses may have been missed`. The second is accurate (the ledger was not written, and a corrupt ledger can never be rewritten by the commands) but reports the read fault as the cause and repeats the first, and its tail ("an identity the memory already uses may have been missed") is about reading and is wrong for a write. Proposed: when the ledger could not be read, do not attempt the write and say nothing more (one warning, the first, with an added tail such as `; it is left as it is and nothing was recorded`), so a corrupt ledger gives one warning and an unwritable one (case 52 shows `not a directory` for both today) still gives its own. That changes the output and the exit code stays 0; it would re-record goldens 50, 51 and 52. Recommendation: do it, as a batch of its own with those goldens, because two identical warnings teach operators to stop reading warnings (the reason `projectid` warns only when it matters), and because skipping a write that is certain to fail changes no file.

Each visible difference is in the switch commit (`0c6b69f`), whose 6 edited pin entries are the diff of the record, and none is a file mode or a persisted format: the record is written and moded as the script left it (an append makes the file at 0666 under the umask, a rewrite leaves it at 0600, as `mktemp` and `mv` did), and the engine's registration record is untouched. (1) **The lock is a file the kernel lets go of, not a directory.** Before: `$STATE_DIR/.installed-targets.lock`, a directory made with `mkdir`, tried 5 times 0.2 s apart and once more, then refused; one older than 5 minutes was taken over with `WARN: longterm-mem: the install-tracking lock at <lock> is older than 5 minutes; treating it as abandoned by a killed run and taking it over`. After: `$STATE_DIR/.installed-targets.flock`, an advisory file lock (mode 0644, made on first use, never removed, as `<registry>.lock` of batch 46) that the engine waits 2 s for; a process that ends, however it ends, holds nothing, so there is no abandoned lock to recognise and no warning. The refusal read `ERROR: longterm-mem: could not acquire the install-tracking lock at $STATE_DIR/.installed-targets.lock; another overlay invocation is updating install state. Nothing was changed — re-run once it finishes, or remove that directory if no other invocation is running.` and reads `ERROR: longterm-mem: could not acquire the install-tracking lock at $STATE_DIR/.installed-targets.flock; another overlay invocation is updating install state. Nothing was changed — re-run once it finishes.` (pins `install/lock-held` and `uninstall/lock-held`; `install/lock-abandoned` and `uninstall/lock-abandoned` lose their `WARN` line and nothing else). It is another name on purpose: a directory a killed run of the script left behind cannot be locked as a file, so it would have wedged every run until someone removed it; now it is garbage that nothing waits for and nothing removes (a test holds that). The alternative is an `mkdir` lock behind the same port, with the staleness heuristics, which is what flock exists to avoid; the file name is the part to change if you want the old one. (2) **The causes the tools of the machine said are said after the sentence.** Before: `mkdir: cannot create directory ...` (or `mktemp: failed to create file via template ...`) on its own line and then `ERROR: longterm-mem: could not create <dir>` (or `... a temporary file in <dir>`). After: only the `ERROR` line, with the system's cause at its end, `... could not create <dir>: not a directory` and `... could not create a temporary file in <dir>: permission denied` (pins `install/record-directory-is-a-file` and `uninstall/record-directory-is-read-only`; the operation and the path an error repeats are left out). The same for a rewrite and an append that fail, and for a record or a binary that cannot be removed: before, `rm`'s own words and the shell stopping with exit 1 (errexit) with the lock directory still there for five minutes; after `ERROR: longterm-mem: could not remove <path>: <cause>`, exit 1, the lock let go (not pinned, as the words are `rm`'s; the before was run on the script of `b4d0aa6` over a read-only `bin/`: `rm: cannot remove '<path>': Permission denied`, exit 1, the lock directory left behind). (3) **The record needs an engine that knows the command.** `ensure_engine_binary` already built the engine on first use and kept going with a warning when it was stale and could not be rebuilt; the tracking used to need none. With a stale engine that cannot be rebuilt, `record`, `release` and `retire` end the run with exit 1 and the engine's own `unknown subcommand`, and `assess` ends with `WARN: longterm-mem: the engine could not say whether any runtime still depends on the shared binary (exit N of 'installed-targets assess'); leaving the registration record and the shared binary untouched. Rebuild the engine with 'labdrian doctor --fix' and re-run uninstall.`, exit 1, nothing removed (fail closed, as an absent record always did). A test holds the three exit codes it can end with. The alternative, keeping the record in bash when the engine is too old, is the duplication this unit removes.

Differences that cannot show on a machine that matters and are listed so that they are not found later: the names are sorted by bytes (`sort -u` sorted by the collation of the locale, which differs only for names with capitals or punctuation under a non-C locale) and a name is ASCII (bash's `[A-Za-z0-9]` under a UTF-8 locale may have matched more); `retire` derives "there is a record" under the lock, where the script used the value it had computed before taking it (they differ only if the file vanished in between, and the engine then keeps the binary); a state directory of `/` shows `/longterm-mem/installed-targets` in the words where the script showed `//longterm-mem/installed-targets` (the file is the same; not pinned, it would write to `/`); `list` is new and used by the harness and by an operator, not by the script (it can be dropped with its test).

  - **Where it went, and why there.** (1) `engine/sha256hex` (domain, pure standard library): `Sum(data)` is the lowercase hex SHA-256 and `IsValid(s)` is exactly 64 lowercase hex characters, byte for byte what `^[0-9a-f]{64}$` accepted. It is a package of its own, not a function of `goal` or `shaper`, because `shaper`, `roles`, `workflow`, `workflowprofile`, `skills`, `projection` and two runtime packages all need it and none should import a sibling for a digest. Six copies of the check (`shaper` clearance, which `shaper.IsSHA256Hex` exported, `roles` handoff, `workflow` event, `skills` approval, `skills` project lock as a loop, `projection` repo key) and eleven of the hash (`shaper` source, `roles` chain, `workflow` event and the lifecycle's two, `workflowprofile` snapshot, `skills` twice, `projection` repo key, `runtime`'s `hashString` with its five callers in the OpenCode and longterm-mem configs, `opencodeprompt`) now call it. The package is named `sha256hex` and not `digest` because every one of those files has a local called `digest`. (2) `Goal.Digest()` in `engine/goal`: the SHA-256 of the canonical `Marshal` bytes, which `workflow` kept as `goalDigest` because the Goal had none. `Create` and `Verify` call it, and so do the tests that used the helper. - **Phase I batch 49 (H34 slice 2: the infrastructure half of the clean-code tail; one owner for a git object name, an accessor for the embedded contract, a propagator that names no contract and one scan of the lines of a registry, a trigger handed its clock and its process runner, one table for the GADU artifacts, and a file-system port for gitprov).** Branch `refactor/phase9-b49` from `5bf48f5`; 18 code and test commits and this ledger commit (the architecture rows of `hexagonal-target.md` are in the same one), none pushed. H34 is done: `hexagonal-target.md` marks it. The engine gained two small packages (69 packages, from 67): `gitobject` (domain) and `synctrigger/osproc` (adapter). Behavior is the same but for the recorded changes under "Decisions stopped on", none of them on the command line.
  - **Where it went, and why there.** (1) `assets`: `AntiGenericDesign` was an exported package variable any caller could assign over. It is `AntiGenericDesign()`, a function over an unexported `//go:embed` variable, and `TestEmbeddedContentsAreNotExportedVariables` reads the source of the package and fails on an exported variable (a test of the source, because no import rule sees an assignment). The three callers (`cmd/contracts.go`, `runtime/opencode_contracts.go`, the tests) call it. The package doc said the contract "will be auto-injected ... once wired by embeddedContract() (see PR-2 of the anti-generic-design-runtime-wiring chain)"; that was done in July, and the doc names who injects it now (`propagate --embedded-contract`, `gate-task`, the OpenCode adapter). (2) `engine/gitobject` (domain, pure standard library): `IsName(s)` is exactly 40 or exactly 64 lowercase hex characters, what `^(?:[0-9a-f]{40}|[0-9a-f]{64})$` accepted. Three copies of that expression decided what a git object name is: `workflow.gitHeadPattern` (a domain), `gitprov.objectName` and `gitfs.hexObjectID` (adapters). It is a package of its own, as `sha256hex` is for a digest, because the dependency rule lets an adapter import a domain and not the other way round, and neither `gitprov` nor `gitfs` should import `workflow` for a string rule; the reason `Provenance.GitHead` must be a full commit id moved from the pattern to the field. (3) `propagator`: the package named two contracts, with constants for the markers of `minimalism-contract` and `anti-generic-design`, a default row label, and a `Config` whose empty marker meant the first contract's. It names none now: `Config` must say its begin marker, its end marker and its row label, `Propagate` refuses one that does not, or whose markers do not start with `<!-- BEGIN:` and `<!-- END:` (`ErrInvalidConfig`, with the registry returned as it came), and `BuildScopedRow` (exported "for testing", with no caller) is gone. The table of the contracts is `cmd`'s (`managedContract` in `cmd/contracts.go`: the name, which is the row label and the stem of the markers, the default path, and the text the binary carries when it carries one; the markers are derived from the name and tests hold their bytes literally, since registries in the field hold those bytes). `propagate` takes its `Config` from the table, and `status`, which read the two begin markers from `propagator`, is handed `ScopedBlock`s (`Service.Blocks`; a `Service` with none panics saying so, as it does for a missing port). The three loops of `hasUnscopedRow`, `replaceUnscopedRow` and `appendToSharedContracts`, each with a flag of its own for being inside a marker block, are one `lineScanner` (`registryLine`: the index, the line, the trimmed line, whether it opens or closes a block, whether it is inside one once read). The `i > 0` of the heading test is gone, provably redundant: at line 0 the line is either the header, which the test excludes, or the section has not been entered. `go.mod` says 1.21, so the iterator is a `Next`/`Line` scanner and not a range over a function. (4) `synctrigger`: the trigger started programs with `os/exec` and read `time.Now`. It takes `Options.Now` and `Options.Runner` now. `Runner` is a port of three calls (`Executable`, `Detach` of a child into a session of its own with the log file for its output, `Run` of a program under a deadline that kills its whole group, answering a `Result` of an exit code or a timeout); the adapter is `synctrigger/osproc`, the one place `os/exec` and `syscall` are reached. The log line is dated by the clock when the sync ended, and the length of a sync is the difference of two readings. A trigger with no `Runner` reports it like any other failure to start something (a `noRunner` whose calls all fail with `no runner was given`), and one with no clock dates its lines with the zero time: it must never fail its caller, and it must never read the machine's clock. `reportUsage` says the usage line, which was written four times, `reportFailure` the others, `absoluteCwd` replaces three steps of checking the cwd in `Run` with one, and the kinds of outcome are constants. `cmd` gives the verb the clock and the `Runner` of its `deps` (`now`, `syncRunner`; nil is the machine's `time.Now` and `osproc.Runner{}`, as every other nil in `deps`). `Detach` no longer opens the null device for standard input: `os/exec` gives a command with no standard input exactly that, and the old code leaked the descriptor. (5) `gadu`: `Artifacts()` is the table of the four files (path and content, built afresh for each caller); `Generate` writes it and `Check` compares the committed files with it in memory. Before, `Check` generated into a scratch directory and read both sides back; it needed a writable temporary directory to say whether four files were right. `ClaudeAgentModel` and `OpenCodeAgentModel` are named as `PiAgentModel` always was, and the description the three agent files share is one constant. The four committed files are byte-identical to what the generator emits (`TestCheck_PassesWhenInSync` against the repository). (6) `gitprov`: the layout of a worktree (`.git` as a directory or a gitfile, what a pointer file says, where a path really leads) is read through an `FS` (`Lstat`, `ReadFile`, `EvalSymlinks`) the `Observer` is given, as git is asked through its `Runner`. Nil is the machine's file system (`OSFS`), so every caller and the 1,000 lines of tests that build an `Observer` without one are unchanged; `Observe`, `Locate` and `cmd` name `OSFS` explicitly.

  - **Decisions stopped on.** None blocks and none is for the owner; four are recorded, not asked, under the rule that an error path nothing could depend on is not a product decision. (1) **Two refusals that did not exist.** `propagator.Propagate` returns `ErrInvalidConfig` for a `Config` with no markers or no row label, or markers that open or close no block; before, an empty marker meant minimalism's, and `cmd` is the only caller and always names all three. `status.Service` panics `status: Service.Blocks is empty`, as it does for a missing port; `cmd` is the only place that builds one. Neither can be reached from a command line. (2) **`gadu-generate --check` no longer needs a temporary directory.** Before, a machine whose temporary directory could not be written answered `creating temp dir: ...` (or `regenerating for check`) and never said whether the files were right; the verdict depends on the content alone now. The words of a missing, stale or unreadable file are the ones they always were (pinned). (3) **The Windows build still fails, in a package of its own.** C4 (the platform split of `synctrigger`) is open and unchanged in scope: `osproc` is the file that will need its platform files, and the trigger no longer imports `syscall`. (4) **Three nils that mean something.** `Observer.FS` nil is the machine's file system (the alternative, a required field, makes three outside callers change, two of them tests of `reviewreceipt/fsstore`, outside this unit's surface); `Options.Now` nil is the zero time and `Options.Runner` nil is a failure to start, said in the log, because the trigger must never fail its caller. A quirk kept, pinned: `replaceUnscopedRow` replaces every unscoped row of the label, each by a whole block (its doc said "the first"), so a registry with two such rows gets two blocks; the next `Propagate` leaves them, since the desired block is there.

They are four rows of `TestOverlayDispatch`, each held to the same four things (its arguments reach the engine verbatim; the exit status of the engine is the overlay's; a home with no engine is refused with "engine binary not found"; `--help` lists it with its own verbs) and workflow's two further help cases are `helpBlocks` of its row. The fake engine is a program written by `overlaytest.StubEngine`. One case is stricter than the bash one: it wants a line that is exactly the argv the engine printed, where the bash case looked for the text inside the output, so an argument the overlay added at the end would fail it. The three readers of text the table uses (`hasLine`, `helpLineAfter`, `helpBlockOf`, ports of `grep -A1 | tail -1` and of the `awk` block) and `engineArgv` have tests of their own. The bash harness of longterm-mem (2,015 lines) is not touched. No test was renamed. (3) **The order is an order of dependency**, and it was found, not chosen: the call graph between the modules has no edge from a module to one after it (the analysis found none among the 69 functions), so each module uses only what the ones before it, and itself, define. `TestAModuleUsesNothingThatALaterModuleDefines` holds it, as `archguard` holds the rings of the engine (it reads the code of each module without its comments and its here-documents, and fails on a later function's name), `TestNoFunctionIsDefinedInTwoModules` holds that the later does not silently replace the earlier, and `TestTheEntryPointDefinesNoFunction` that the entry point stays thin. (4) **The loader** is an array of names and a loop at the top level of the entry point, and not a function: `declare -A TARGET_PATHS` in a sourced file inside a function would make the array local to it. Three other shapes were rejected: one `source` line for each module with a `# shellcheck source=` directive (so that `shellcheck -x` follows them; the list would be written twice, once to check the file is there and once to source it, and the order could not be read by a test), a glob of `bin/lib/*.sh` (a module that is missing would be silent and the order would be the alphabet's), and a `load_module` function (the function-local arrays). `lib/` is beside the REAL location of the script (`SCRIPT_DIR`, symlinks resolved) and never from `OVERLAY_DIR`, which the tests and a person with another checkout point elsewhere. A module that is missing is two lines on stderr (the name, the place it should be, and `git checkout -- bin/lib`) and exit 1, before anything has run, run or sourced. The loader uses only builtins, so the PATH of the smoke test of CI (bash, dirname, readlink, no go) still loads it, and `TestTheScriptLoadsWithOnlyBashDirnameAndReadlinkOnThePath` holds that.
